topPRs.title: feat(kona): execute NUT bundles at Karst fork activation
topPRs.author: maurelian
topPRs.body:
## Summary

Wires Karst NUT bundle execution into kona-node's payload derivation, matching op-node's behavior.

- `kona-hardforks` gets a `build.rs` that reads `op-core/nuts/bundles/karst_nut_bundle.json` at compile time and emits Rust code constructing the `NutBundle` — keeps the crate `no_std` and serde-free at runtime.
- The `Hardfork` trait grows `upgrade_gas()`; the stateful attributes builder adds that gas to the block gas limit when Karst activates, so upgrade transactions have headroom.
- Test in `forks.rs` updated from `len() == 0` to `len() == 32` to reflect the populated bundle.

## Stacking

Stacked on top of #20062 (PR 1 — NUT bundle types in `op-alloy-consensus`). The first two commits belong to that PR and will drop out on rebase once #20062 merges. Review only `c38d4300d8`.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo nextest run` in `rust/kona` — 119 passed
- [x] `test_karst_upgrade_txs` asserts 32 transactions
- [x] `test_karst_upgrade_gas` asserts 51_600_000 gas
- [ ] Waiting on #20062 to merge, then rebase onto develop

topPRs.title: test(op-acceptance-tests): add EIP-7934 block size limit disabled test
topPRs.author: joshklop
topPRs.body:
Assert that OP Stack chains can build blocks exceeding the EIP-7934 10 MiB RLP block size limit. Submits many transactions with large calldata under a 200M gas limit and verifies a single block exceeds 10 MiB in total transaction data.

Also adds WithGasLimit to L2Configurator and WithL2GasLimit deployer option to support custom L2 block gas limits in tests.

Stacked on #20068

topPRs.title: test(op-reth): guard negotiated eth wire protocol version
topPRs.author: joshklop
topPRs.body:
Add an integration test that spins up two op-reth nodes, lets them complete the devp2p handshake, and asserts the negotiated eth subprotocol version is exactly 69.

The test is intentionally written to fail when upstream reth bumps the negotiated version (e.g. to eth/70). That failure is the signal: it forces a conscious review of the new version's behavior before we ship it, rather than silently inheriting a protocol change on the next reth bump.
